title: Hangover IV Drip: Does It Work, What It Costs, and When to Skip It
excerpt: Do hangover IV drips work? What's in the bag, typical $150-300 cost, how to find a safe provider near you or in Vegas, the risks, and when to go to the ER instead.
metaDescription: Do hangover IV drips work? What is in the bag, what it costs ($150-300), how to find a safe provider, the risks, and when to go to the ER instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a hangover IV drip will probably make you feel somewhat better, mostly because it puts about a liter of fluid into you quickly and often includes anti-nausea and pain medicine that work fast. What it won't do is "flush" alcohol out of your body, speed up your liver, or fix the main causes of a hangover. There is no good evidence from controlled trials that IV therapy cures hangovers better than drinking fluids, eating, taking an over-the-counter pain reliever, and sleeping. Most drips cost somewhere around $150 to $300, more with add-ons or a hotel visit. For a healthy adult who can't keep water down and has somewhere important to be, it can be a reasonable splurge. For everyone else, a sports drink, breakfast, and a nap get you most of the way for a few dollars.

**The quick rules:** An IV drip is a medical procedure, not a spa treatment, so use a service where a licensed clinician screens you first and a nurse or paramedic places the line. Tell them what you drank, what medicines you take, and any heart, kidney, or liver problems. And know when an IV lounge is the wrong place to be: if someone is confused, can't stay awake, is breathing slowly, or keeps vomiting while drowsy, that is possible alcohol poisoning and needs 911 or an emergency room, not a drip bar.

> **When to see a doctor or go to the ER instead.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if someone is confused, can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or very pale skin, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. These are signs of alcohol poisoning (see our [alcohol poisoning signs guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs)). **See a doctor promptly** if you've been vomiting for more than about a day and can't keep fluids down, see blood in your vomit or stool, have severe belly pain, chest pain, or a racing heartbeat that won't settle, or if you develop shaking, sweating, anxiety, or hallucinations a day or two after heavy drinking. That last group can be alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical problem that needs real care, not a vitamin drip. If you have heart failure, kidney disease, or take blood pressure or heart medicine, talk to your doctor before booking an IV.

## What's Actually in a Hangover IV Bag

Hangover drips have catchy names on the menu ("Recovery," "Revive," "The Morning After"), but the ingredients come from a fairly short list. Knowing it helps you decide what's worth paying for.

**The base: about a liter of fluid.** Almost every drip starts with a bag of saline (salt water, sodium chloride 0.9%) or lactated Ringer's (a salt solution with potassium, calcium, and lactate that's closer to the makeup of blood). This is the part that does most of the work. A typical bag is 500 ml to 1 liter, given over 30 to 60 minutes.

**Vitamins.** Most add a B-complex (often including thiamine, B6, and B12) and vitamin C. Some use a version of the "Myers' cocktail," a mix of magnesium, calcium, B vitamins, and vitamin C that has been used in alternative medicine since the 1970s. Some menus also offer glutathione, an antioxidant, as a separate add-on.

**Medicines (the parts you actually feel).** This is where drips differ most, and where the fast relief usually comes from:

- **Anti-nausea medicine**, most commonly ondansetron (brand name Zofran). It's a prescription drug used in hospitals and works quickly when given by IV.
- **An anti-inflammatory pain reliever**, often ketorolac (Toradol), a prescription-strength NSAID in the same family as ibuprofen.
- **A stomach acid reducer**, often famotidine (Pepcid), for heartburn and an upset stomach.

**What the bag doesn't contain:** anything that breaks down alcohol faster. Your liver clears alcohol at its own pace, and nothing in a standard drip changes that.

## Does a Hangover IV Actually Work?

It depends on what you mean by "work." Here's what we can say with reasonable confidence.

### The fluid helps with one piece of the problem

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing vasopressin, a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Add sweating, vomiting, and not drinking water, and many people wake up mildly dehydrated. Replacing fluid can ease thirst, dizziness when you stand up, a dry mouth, and some of the headache.

But dehydration is only one part of a hangover, and probably not the biggest one. Researchers who study hangovers, including the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have pointed out that hangover severity doesn't line up neatly with measures of dehydration. The main drivers seem to be the body's inflammatory response to alcohol, the build-up and clearance of acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), disrupted sleep, low blood sugar in some people, and irritation of the stomach lining. A liter of saline doesn't touch most of those.

### The medicines help with symptoms, fast

If you're vomiting and can't keep anything down, an IV is genuinely useful. Oral medicine and water just come back up, while IV ondansetron and IV fluid go straight into your bloodstream. The same goes for pain relief: ketorolac given by IV acts faster than a pill. A lot of the "I felt like a new person in 45 minutes" stories come from this combination, not from the vitamins.

That's worth knowing because you can get similar effects in other ways. Drinking fluids slowly, taking an over-the-counter antacid, and an over-the-counter pain reliever with food will often get you to a similar place, just more slowly.

### The vitamins are the weakest link

There's no good evidence that IV vitamins improve a hangover in a healthy, well-fed adult. Your body gets rid of extra water-soluble vitamins like B and C in urine, so a large dose mostly ends up in the toilet. The one real exception is thiamine (vitamin B1) in people who drink heavily over long periods and are actually deficient. That's a medical situation that doctors treat in hospitals, not a reason for an occasional drinker to buy a drip.

Glutathione add-ons are the same story. It's an important antioxidant inside your cells, and the liver uses it to handle some toxins. But there's no good evidence that an IV dose of glutathione makes a hangover go away faster.

### What the research looks like overall

There are very few controlled trials of IV therapy for hangovers in healthy people, and none that we're aware of that are large and well designed enough to settle the question. Broader reviews of hangover treatments, such as a 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* by Pittler, Verster, and Ernst, concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary treatment prevents or cures hangovers. Later reviews have reached similar conclusions: some remedies show hints of benefit in small studies, but the overall quality of evidence is low.

In emergency medicine, IV fluids are given to intoxicated patients mainly to treat dehydration or low blood pressure. A small emergency-department trial found that giving IV saline to intoxicated patients didn't speed up how quickly they sobered up, which fits what we know about liver metabolism.

**Bottom line on effectiveness:** an IV can relieve dehydration, nausea, and pain quickly. There is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover overall, and the extras are mostly marketing.

## How Much Does a Hangover IV Cost?

Prices vary a lot by city, clinic type, and what's in the bag. These are general ranges, not quotes, so always check the menu and ask what's included.

| What you're paying for | Typical price range (US) |
|---|---|
| Basic hydration bag (fluids only, sometimes with a B vitamin) | Roughly $100 to $200 |
| Standard "hangover" drip (fluids, vitamins, anti-nausea medicine) | Roughly $150 to $300 |
| Premium or "VIP" drips (bigger bags, more medicines, glutathione) | Often $250 to $400 or more |
| Individual add-ons (extra anti-nausea, pain relief, glutathione, B12 shot) | Often $25 to $75 each |
| Mobile service to your home or hotel | Base price plus a travel fee, often higher per person for solo bookings |

A few cost points people miss:

- **Insurance almost never pays.** Elective IV hydration for a hangover is treated as a wellness service. Expect to pay out of pocket. Some places accept HSA or FSA cards, but check with your plan first, because a hangover drip may not count as a qualifying medical expense.
- **Group pricing exists.** Bachelor and bachelorette parties often get per-person discounts on mobile visits.
- **Tips and fees add up.** Hotel visits in tourist cities may add a service fee, and some places charge more on weekends and holidays.
- **Compare it with the alternative.** An urgent care visit for vomiting and dehydration might be billed to insurance, and the clinicians there will actually look for other causes. If you're truly unwell, that can be the better value.

## How to Find a Safe Hangover IV Near You

Searching "hangover IV near me" turns up a mix of medical clinics, IV lounges, med spas, and mobile services. Quality varies. Here's how to tell a careful operation from a risky one.

**Green flags:**

- **A licensed medical director** (a physician or, in some states, a nurse practitioner) oversees the service and is named on the website.
- **A real health screening before the drip.** Someone asks about your medical history, medicines, allergies, and how much you drank, and checks your blood pressure and heart rate. In many states a clinician has to approve each patient.
- **A registered nurse or paramedic places the IV**, using sterile technique and single-use supplies.
- **Clear ingredient lists with doses** on the menu, and staff who can explain them.
- **Someone monitors you** during the drip, and you're told what to watch for afterward.

**Red flags:**

- Claims that the drip "detoxes" alcohol, "flushes your liver," or "cures" a hangover.
- No questions asked about your health, or a quick form with nobody reviewing it.
- Unclear who the medical director is, or no way to reach a clinician after you leave.
- Pressure to add expensive extras you didn't ask about.
- A willingness to treat someone who is still visibly very drunk. A responsible provider will turn them away or send them to an emergency room.

Rules for IV hydration businesses vary by state. In general, IV therapy is treated as the practice of medicine or nursing, and state boards have taken action against operators who skipped proper oversight. Asking "who's your medical director, and who reviews my intake form?" is a fair question and a quick way to filter out weak services.

## Hangover IVs in Las Vegas (and Other Party Cities)

Las Vegas is probably the most famous place for hangover IVs. The Strip has walk-in IV lounges, and many mobile services will come to your hotel room, sometimes around the clock. Similar services are common in Miami, Nashville, Scottsdale, New Orleans, and other bachelor-party destinations.

A few tips specific to tourist cities:

- **Book early on weekends.** Saturday and Sunday mornings are the busiest times, and popular mobile services can fill up.
- **Check your hotel's rules.** Most hotels allow licensed mobile services, but you'll need to give your room number and be present.
- **Watch the "per person" pricing for groups.** Make sure you know whether the quoted price covers one drip or the whole group, and whether the travel fee is split.
- **Desert heat matters.** In Vegas or Scottsdale in summer, you may be more dehydrated than you realize after a day at a pool party. Drink water through the day so you don't need a drip in the first place.
- **Don't skip the screening because you're on vacation.** The same health questions apply. If you take blood pressure medicine, blood thinners, or antidepressants, mention it.

If you're planning a trip and want fewer mornings that need fixing, our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter most: pacing, eating before you drink, alternating with water, and getting real sleep.

## Risks and Side Effects of IV Hangover Treatment

For most healthy adults, a properly given IV is low risk. But it isn't zero risk, and the risks are higher at places that cut corners.

**Common, usually minor:**

- Bruising, soreness, or a small bump at the needle site
- A cold feeling in the arm as the fluid goes in
- A metallic taste or flushing from some vitamins
- Needing to pee a lot afterward

**Less common, more serious:**

- **Infiltration.** The fluid leaks into the tissue around the vein, causing swelling and pain.
- **Phlebitis or infection.** The vein becomes inflamed, or bacteria get in if the technique wasn't sterile. Redness that spreads, warmth, pus, or fever afterward needs medical attention.
- **Fluid overload.** In people with heart failure or kidney disease, a liter of fluid given quickly can strain the heart and cause swelling or shortness of breath. This is why the health screening matters.
- **Allergic reactions** to a vitamin or medicine in the bag.
- **Medicine-specific risks.** Ketorolac is a strong NSAID. Combined with recent drinking and dehydration, it can irritate the stomach and stress the kidneys, and it isn't suitable for people with ulcers, kidney problems, or bleeding risks, or for those on blood thinners. Ondansetron can affect heart rhythm in some people and interacts with certain medicines, including some antidepressants.

**The hidden risk: a drip can mask something serious.** Severe vomiting and belly pain after drinking are usually a bad hangover, but they can also be pancreatitis, a stomach bleed, or alcohol poisoning. An IV lounge isn't set up to diagnose those. If your symptoms feel worse than any hangover you've had, an urgent care or ER is the safer choice.

## Who Should Skip the Drip

Talk to a doctor first, or choose an urgent care or ER, if you:

- Have **heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease**
- Have **high blood pressure** or take heart or blood pressure medicines
- Take **blood thinners**, or have a stomach ulcer or bleeding problem (especially relevant if the drip includes ketorolac)
- Take medicines that affect heart rhythm, or antidepressants that can interact with ondansetron
- Are **pregnant**
- Are still **noticeably intoxicated**
- Drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop. That can be withdrawal, and it needs proper medical care rather than a wellness drip.

## Cheaper Alternatives That Get You Most of the Way

If you can keep fluids down, you can usually get much of the benefit of an IV for a few dollars. Oral rehydration (drinking a fluid with the right balance of salt and sugar) is the standard treatment for mild to moderate dehydration worldwide, because your gut absorbs it efficiently.

**A simple morning-after plan:**

1. **Sip, don't chug.** Drink an electrolyte drink or water in small, steady sips, especially if your stomach is unsettled. Large gulps are more likely to come back up.
2. **Pick a drink with sodium.** Plain water is fine, but a drink with salt and a little sugar helps your body hold onto it. Our [electrolyte drinks for hangover comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) and [Pedialyte vs Gatorade guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) cover which ones are worth buying, and our [Liquid IV for hangover review](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) looks at the popular powder.
3. **Settle your stomach.** Bland food like toast, crackers, bananas, or rice is easiest. An antacid can help with heartburn. For more, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).
4. **Treat the headache carefully.** An over-the-counter pain reliever taken with food can help. Ibuprofen is harder on the stomach after drinking, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds strain to the liver, so take one standard dose and follow the label. Our [hangover headache guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) goes through the options.
5. **Sleep.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, and a lot of hangover misery is plain exhaustion. Even an extra hour or two helps.

Most hangovers ease within 24 hours either way. Our guide to [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains what affects recovery time.

### When an IV makes more sense than a sports drink

An IV is most reasonable when you've been vomiting and can't keep even small sips down, you have something important that day (a flight, a wedding, a big meeting), and you're otherwise healthy with no heart or kidney issues. If the vomiting has gone on for a long time, or you feel truly ill rather than just hungover, go to urgent care instead. They can give IV fluids and anti-nausea medicine too, and they can check for problems an IV lounge can't.

## Prevention Beats a $250 Morning

The cheapest hangover IV is the one you don't need. A few things reliably make the next morning easier:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies. Drinking faster than that builds up alcohol in your blood.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks keeps you hydrated and slows you down.
- **Stick to clearer drinks if dark ones hit you hard.** Some people find drinks like bourbon or red wine give them worse hangovers, possibly because of compounds called congeners.
- **Hydrate before bed.** A glass or two of an electrolyte drink before sleep can save you a lot of trouble in the morning.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare brands. Like an IV, it isn't a substitute for drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

- A hangover IV usually contains about a liter of saline or lactated Ringer's, B vitamins and vitamin C, and often anti-nausea, pain, and acid-reducing medicine.
- It can relieve dehydration, nausea, and headache quickly, especially if you can't keep fluids down. There is no good evidence that it removes alcohol faster or shortens a hangover overall.
- Expect to pay roughly $150 to $300 for a standard drip, more for add-ons or hotel visits. Insurance rarely covers it.
- Choose a service with a named medical director, a real health screening, and a nurse or paramedic placing the line.
- Skip the drip bar and go to an ER for signs of alcohol poisoning, prolonged vomiting, blood in vomit, severe pain, or shaking and hallucinations after heavy drinking.
- For an ordinary hangover, an electrolyte drink, food, a careful dose of pain reliever, and sleep get you most of the way for a fraction of the cost.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does a hangover IV drip actually work?**

It can help you feel better faster, mainly by replacing fluid and, in many drips, giving anti-nausea and pain medicine directly into your vein. That's especially useful if you can't keep water down. But there is no good evidence from controlled trials that an IV shortens a hangover overall or works better than oral fluids, food, an over-the-counter pain reliever, and rest. It doesn't remove alcohol from your body any faster.

**How much does a hangover IV cost?**

In the US, a standard hangover drip usually runs about $150 to $300. Basic hydration-only bags can be cheaper, while premium drips with extra medicines or glutathione can cost $250 to $400 or more. Add-ons often cost $25 to $75 each, and mobile visits to your home or hotel usually add a travel fee. Insurance rarely covers hangover IVs, so expect to pay out of pocket.

**What's in a hangover IV bag?**

Most contain 500 ml to 1 liter of saline or lactated Ringer's, plus vitamins such as a B-complex and vitamin C. Many also include ondansetron (Zofran) for nausea, ketorolac (Toradol) for pain and inflammation, and famotidine (Pepcid) for stomach acid. Some offer magnesium or glutathione add-ons. The fluid and medicines do most of the work; there's little evidence the vitamins add much for a healthy person.

**How long does a hangover IV take to work?**

The drip itself usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. Many people notice less nausea and headache within that time, because IV medicines act quickly. Fatigue and brain fog from poor sleep often linger, since an IV can't replace rest.

**Is a hangover IV safe?**

For most healthy adults, an IV given by a licensed nurse or paramedic after a proper health screening is low risk. Possible problems include bruising, vein irritation, infection, allergic reactions, and side effects from the medicines in the bag. People with heart failure, kidney or liver disease, high blood pressure, or those on blood thinners or certain antidepressants should talk to a doctor first. Never use an IV lounge in place of emergency care for signs of alcohol poisoning.

**Can an IV drip sober you up faster?**

No. Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, and IV fluids don't speed that up. A small emergency-department study found that IV saline didn't shorten the time it took intoxicated patients to sober up. A reputable IV provider should not treat someone who is still very drunk.

**When should I go to the ER instead of an IV lounge?**

Go to an emergency room or call 911 if someone is confused, hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or very pale skin, has a seizure, or vomits while barely conscious. See a doctor promptly for vomiting lasting more than about a day, blood in vomit or stool, severe belly or chest pain, or shaking, sweating, and hallucinations a day or two after heavy drinking. An IV lounge can't diagnose or treat these problems.

**Are hangover IVs in Las Vegas worth it?**

They're widely available on the Strip and through mobile services that come to your hotel, so they're convenient. Whether they're worth $150 to $300 depends on how sick you feel. If you can keep fluids down, an electrolyte drink, breakfast, and sleep will usually get you most of the way. If you're vomiting and have a flight or event that day, a drip from a properly supervised service can be a reasonable choice.
